## Introduction

This document serves as a lab report for lan 6 in the Advanced R programming course (732A94) autumn 2026. This lab focuses on comparing different techniques for improving the R code execution time. The techniques are applied to the knapsack (1-0) problem.

We use a brute force search algorithm, a dynamic programming algorithm, and a "greedy" (approximative) algorithm, in different version, measuring and comparing their respective performances. Questions from the lab assignment are answered for each algorithm/

## Brute force search

The brute force search checks every possible combination of objects. In this version two variables are used to keep track of the best solution so far, comparing this to the next check, and updating it if the next combination is better.

We use the base function ìntToBits() to create a representation each combination (using the binary representation of all numbers from 0 up to n-1, where n is the number of available objects to choose from).

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
brute_force_knapsack <- function(x,W) {

  # / input validation code not shown here, see source code in package/ *

  # n items
  n <- nrow(x)

  # Extract the item weights and values as plain vectors
  weights <- x$w
  values <- x$v

  # variables to keep track of the best solution
  best_value    <- 0
  best_elements <- integer(0)

  # Generate all possible combinations of items
  for (i in 0:(2^n - 1)) {
    # Logical combination in binary representation ex: {000, 001, ..., 111} for n = 3
    combination <- as.logical(intToBits(i)[seq_len(n)])
    total_weight <- sum(weights[combination])   # sum all TRUE values
    total_value  <- sum(values[combination])    # sum all TRUE values

    # Check if the combination is valid and better than the best found so far
    if (total_weight <= W & total_value > best_value) {
      best_value    <- total_value
      best_elements <- which(combination)
    }
  }

  # Return the result in a list
  list(value = round(best_value), elements = best_elements)
}

```

*How much time does it take to run the algorithm for n = 16 objects?*

```{r}
knapsack_objects <- random_numbers_for_knapsack()

# Run bench::mark() once for every combination of the parameters
runs <- bench::press(
  n = c(8, 12, 16, 20),
  W = 3500,
  {
    bench::mark(brute_force_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects[1:n, ], W = W),
                filter_gc = FALSE)
  },
  .quiet = TRUE
)

# Show the results in a table
runs[, c("n", "W", "min", "median", "itr/sec", "mem_alloc")]
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
cat("It takes about", format(runs$median[runs$n == 16]), "(median)")
```

## Dynamic programming

The dynamic programming version is based on an algorithm described on [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knapsack_problem#Dynamic_programming_in-advance_algorithm "Knapsack algorithms"). Here we create a matrix which the algorithm then walks through line by line, comparing object combinations, having the best one ready when the last element is processed.

```{r, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
knapsack_dynamic <- function(x,W){

  # / input validation code not shown here, see source code in package/ *

  # n items
  n <- nrow(x)

  # row and column for zero objects/capacity
  M <- matrix(0, nrow = n + 1, ncol = W + 1)

  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    for (w in 0:W) {

      # row i+1 in matrix corresponds to object i in x
      if (x$w[i] > w) {
        M[i + 1, w + 1] <- M[i, w + 1]
      } else {
        exclude <- M[i, w + 1]
        include <- x$v[i] + M[i, w - x$w[i] + 1]

        M[i + 1, w + 1] <- max(exclude, include)
      }
    }
  }

  best_value <- M[n+1, W+1]

  # trace back to find which items are selected
  items_selected <- integer(0)
  for (i in n:1) {

    if (M[i + 1, w + 1] != M[i, w + 1]) {

      # object i was included
      items_selected <- c(i, items_selected)

      # subtract its weight
      w <- w - x$w[i]
    }
  }

  return(list(value = best_value, items = items_selected))


}

```

*How much time does it take to run the algorithm for n = 500 objects?*

```{r}
res_dynamic <- bench::mark(knapsack_dynamic(x = knapsack_objects[1:500, ], W = 3500),
                           filter_gc = FALSE)

res_dynamic[, c("min", "median", "itr/sec", "mem_alloc")]
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
cat("It takes about", format(res_dynamic$median), "(median)")
```

## Greedy heuristic

The greedy heuristic algorithm calculates "value per weight unit" for each of the objects, sorts the result in descending order, and then starts picking objects from the top. The result will not necessarily be the optimal total knapsack value, but the algorithm promises to do the task quickly!

```{r, eval = FALSE; echo = TRUE}

greedy_knapsack <- function(x, W) {
  # / input validation code not shown here, see source code in package/ *
  
  # Value per unit of weight for every item sorted best to worst
  ratio <- x$v / x$w
  item_order <- order(ratio, decreasing = TRUE)
  
  # Running total weight for the items added in that order
  running_weight <- cumsum(x$w[item_order])
  
  # All items less than or equal to the capacity fit in the knapsack
  fits <- running_weight <= W
  
  # Keep the rows that fit and add up their values
  selected_items <- item_order[fits]
  total_value    <- sum(x$v[selected_items])
  
  return(list(value = round(total_value), elements = selected_items))
}

```

*How much time does it take to run the algorithm for n = 1,000,000 objects?*

```{r}
knapsack_objects_large <- suppressWarnings(random_numbers_for_knapsack(n = 1e6))

res_greed <- bench::mark(greedy_knapsack(x = knapsack_objects_large, W = 3500),
                         filter_gc = FALSE)

res_greed[, c("min", "median", "itr/sec", "mem_alloc")]
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
cat("It takes about", format(res_greed$median), "(median)")
```

## Profiling and optimizing the code

*What performance gain could you get by trying to improve your code?*

Base R (`a`) vs tidyverse (`b`) versions, relative to the fastest (= 1).

```{r}
compare_functions(greedy_knapsack, greedy_knapsack_tidyverse,
                  args = list(x = knapsack_objects_large, W = 3500))$timings

compare_functions(brute_force_knapsack, brute_force_knapsack_tidyverse,
                  args = list(x = knapsack_objects[1:12, ], W = 3500))$timings
```

Brute force keeping only the best so far (`a`) vs saving all combinations in a data.frame (`b`).

```{r}
compare_functions(brute_force_knapsack, brute_force_knapsack_df,
                  args = list(x = knapsack_objects[1:12, ], W = 3500))$timings
```

Brute force with a loop (`a`) vs all combinations as a 0/1 matrix and matrix products (`b`).

```{r}
compare_functions(brute_force_knapsack, brute_force_knapsack_matrix,
                  args = list(x = knapsack_objects[1:12, ], W = 3500))$timings
```
